title: Orcas Turn Sunfish Into Piñatas, Scientists Discover
summary:
Orcas are known for brutal hunting tactics — slapping stingrays, punting seals into the air, and otherwise playing with their food. Now scientists have documented something even stranger: orcas smashing sunfish like piñatas.

In 2024 and 2025, researchers watched this behavior in the Gulf of California. In both cases, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca then slammed into it with enough force to smash the fish to smithereens. The findings appeared July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand who wasn't involved in the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen." She had seen a few social media videos of orcas battering sunfish, but the new paper does a deep dive into the behavior.

Nyegaard isn't surprised that orcas found a creative way to handle sharp-tail sunfish. Those massive fish can reach a few meters — about 10 feet — long. "Orcas will do all sorts of things," she said. "They are so clever at figuring out how to hunt and deal with a ton of different prey types."

Hunting is often a team sport for orcas. They band together to ambush blue whales and whale sharks, and they team up to make waves that knock penguins off ice.

Why pulverize a sunfish? Francesca Pancaldi, a marine biologist at Mexico's National Polytechnic Institute, says orcas most likely smash them into small pieces to help feed their young. After one of the explosions described in the paper, a young orca fed on the small bits.

But feeding may not be the only reason. "Killer whales are highly social animals," Pancaldi said. A single activity can provide nutrition, help orcas bond, and offer a way for young orcas to learn how to hunt.
why_it_matters: The discovery shows that even a well-known predator still surprises scientists, and it strengthens the idea that orcas pass hunting techniques between generations like culture — which matters for how we protect populations whose survival depends on learned skills, not instinct alone.

background_read: Orcas (also called killer whales — they are actually the largest members of the dolphin family) live in every ocean and hunt in tightly bonded family groups. Different populations specialise in different prey: some eat fish, others hunt seals, dolphins or even large whales. Biologists think these hunting habits are cultural, learned from older relatives rather than built in at birth.

The Gulf of California (the narrow sea between Mexico's mainland and the Baja California peninsula, also known as the Sea of Cortez) is one of the most species-rich stretches of water on Earth and a long-time natural laboratory for marine biologists. It is also a hotspot for sunfish.

Sharp-tail sunfish are huge, flat-bodied relatives of the ocean sunfish, the heaviest bony fish in the world. Ocean sunfish are famously covered in parasites and often lie near the surface so that seabirds can pick the parasites off. Marianne Nyegaard (a marine biologist at Auckland Museum in New Zealand, who identified a new sunfish species in 2017 after years of searching for it) is a leading expert on the group. Frontiers in Ethology, where the new paper appeared, is a journal devoted to the study of animal behaviour — a field that increasingly focuses on how animals learn skills from each other.

perspectives.description: The behaviour is a striking example of animals inventing new tactics and probably teaching them to their young. It also suggests orcas waste little: a sunfish that could be hard to bite into becomes bite-sized food for a calf. Each new documented behaviour helps researchers map how much orca groups differ from one another.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — too few observations to explain
perspectives.description: Only two cases are described, and calling it a piñata or 'play' risks reading human ideas into animal behaviour. The feeding-the-young explanation is a reasonable hypothesis, not proof — orcas may simply be practising a strike on a slow, harmless target. Scientists need many more sightings before claiming a pattern.

Sunfish are slow, parasite-ridden and often float near the surface, which makes them unusually convenient objects for experiments in hunting. Orcas worldwide split into ecotypes with different diets and techniques, so a Gulf of California group handling a large, awkward prey item fits an existing pattern rather than breaking it.

Researchers will want drone footage and repeat observations to see whether the technique spreads through the pod or fades away. If it is cultural, it could appear in other orca groups too. Meanwhile, it raises a question for the Gulf of California: how much extra pressure do these smashings put on a sunfish population already living in a busy, warming sea?
